battle.title: Undo Button: Backtracking Gauntlet
battle.description: Base cases, call order and choose-explore-unchoose under pressure.

questions.text: A recursive method has no base case. What happens when it is called?
options: It throws StackOverflowError after the call stack fills up
It loops forever using constant memory
The compiler refuses to compile it
questions.answer: It throws StackOverflowError after the call stack fills up
questions.explanation: Every call adds a stack frame and none ever returns, so the finite stack runs out. Java does not optimise away recursion, so it does not run forever in constant memory, and the compiler cannot detect a missing base case.

The first println runs on the way down (3, 2, 1) and the second runs as the calls return, in reverse order of calling: 10, 20, 30. The tempting reversed first half forgets that the call happens after the first print.

questions.text: You must list every possible ordering of 4 distinct items. Which technique is the natural fit?
options: Backtracking: choose an unused item, recurse, then unchoose it
A sliding window over the items
A single for loop that swaps neighbours once
questions.answer: Backtracking: choose an unused item, recurse, then unchoose it
questions.explanation: Permutations are built position by position, so you need to try each unused item, explore, and undo the choice to try the next. A sliding window or one pass of swaps cannot enumerate all orderings, and binary search needs a monotonic answer.
The subsets of {1..5} that sum to 5 are {5}, {1,4} and {2,3}. Choosing 'take or skip' at each index explores them all; 2 forgets the single-element subset {5}.

questions.text: Roughly how much work does it take to generate all permutations of n distinct items?
options: About n! permutations, each costing about n to build or copy
questions.answer: About n! permutations, each costing about n to build or copy
questions.explanation: There are n! permutations and just writing each one out costs n, so the work is on the order of n * n!. 2^n counts subsets, not orderings, and polynomial answers are far too small.

coding.description: Given a string of distinct lowercase letters, print every permutation of its letters, one per line, in lexicographic (alphabetical) order. The input letters may come in any order.
coding.inputDescription: A single line with the distinct letters.
coding.outputDescription: All permutations, one per line, in lexicographic order.
coding.constraints: 1 <= length <= 6, letters are distinct lowercase a-z

debug.title: The Subset That Never Undid Itself
debug.description: Given distinct positive integers in ascending order and a target, print every subset (in ascending order, one per line, elements separated by spaces) whose sum equals the target, in depth-first order. Print none if there is no such subset. The output contains wrong or extra subsets. Input: line 1 'n target', line 2 the n integers.
hints: Try 5 5 with 1 2 3 4 5. Expected: 1 4, then 2 3, then 5. What is printed instead? Do the subsets contain numbers they should not?
Look at how cur changes inside the loop in go(). After the recursive call returns, what is cur?
cur.add(...) is never matched by a removal, so choices from earlier branches leak into later ones.
After the recursive call, remove the last element (cur.remove(cur.size() - 1)) to undo the choice before trying the next value.
